docs.title: Scratchsmith
docs.text:
The daemonless supply-chain packager for prebuilt dynamic Linux binaries.

Point Scratchsmith at a dynamically linked glibc ELF binary, or a musl/Alpine one on x86_64, and get a minimal FROM scratch OCI image. You need no Dockerfile and no static-linking prerequisite. It resolves the binary's shared libraries the way the loader does (RPATH/RUNPATH/$ORIGIN, the interpreter, versioned soname symlinks). For glibc it stages the pieces nothing else remembers (NSS modules, a working nsswitch.conf, minimal passwd/group). Then it assembles a non-root image with reproducible layers.

docs.title: Why not just static-link + FROM scratch?
docs.text:
If you can rebuild your service as a static binary (CGO_ENABLED=0, musl), do that. You need no packer. Scratchsmith is built for the binaries that static linking cannot help:

  • Closed-source or vendor binaries you cannot recompile.
  • glibc binaries that rely on NSS, dlopen, or locale behavior. Static glibc breaks these quietly, often only in production.
  • Anything where "just rebuild it static" is not on the table.

That is the wedge, and it is not a fence. Scratchsmith already packs a static binary too, because the resolver detects it and stages the single file. When you want an SBOM, a hardening report, a non-root image, and no Dockerfile, it is equally handy. More: Comparison & limitations.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Resolve: emulate the ld.so search order from the ELF itself (RPATH is transitive, RUNPATH is not, $ORIGIN is per-object). An object that has RUNPATH searches no RPATH, neither its own nor one it inherits. A name that an object loaded earlier already carries, as the name it was needed by or as its DT_SONAME, resolves to that object with no search, as ld.so does. A library found through a symlink expands $ORIGIN to the directory that holds the symlink, as ld.so does, and stages from its real file. Each RPATH or RUNPATH string is a : list, and its entries are searched in order. A file of another ELF class or machine than the binary, such as a 32-bit copy in lib ahead of the 64-bit one in lib64, is skipped and the search goes on, as ld.so skips it. When every copy is of another arch, or the binary names the file by path, that file still stages, and a warning says the image cannot load it. An empty entry means the directory the program starts in. A build cannot know that directory, so Scratchsmith does not search an empty entry. If the split entries miss, a string that holds : is also tried whole as one directory, before the default directories. The loader finds a DT_NEEDED library there only through the image's ld.so.cache. If ldconfig does not cache the library under the needed name, Scratchsmith does not take it. The name must start with lib or ld- and hold .so, or start with ld.so. or ld64.so.. The library's own soname must be that name, or absent. An --include file in that directory stages with no such check. Three kinds of entry are searched here as they always were, though ld.so does not search them: a wholly empty string (read as $ORIGIN), a relative entry (read against the object's directory, where ld.so reads it against the working directory), and a name glued to a token, such as $ORIGINX or $ORIGIN_x (expanded, where ld.so keeps it literal). A library found only through such an entry loads from the image's ld.so.cache, if ldconfig caches it under the needed name by the rule above. pack prints one note on stderr for the entry, and the note names any library that the cache does not list, which the image then cannot load. On x86_64, $PLATFORM is read as x86_64, and on aarch64 as aarch64. On any other architecture the token has no value, and a search path that holds it fails the pack wherever the loader would search it. glibc reads it as haswell or xeon_phi on some Intel CPUs, but those copies are optimized builds that not every CPU can run, so they never stage. A library missing as x86_64 but present under such a name gets a hint, and a library that ships while ld.so on such a CPU would load such a copy gets a note on stderr. $LIB takes the value the glibc in the host root uses, read from the directory where the first libc.so.6 of the binary's arch sits, without a leading usr/: lib/x86_64-linux-gnu on Debian and Ubuntu, lib64 on Fedora, lib on Arch. When that value is not lib64 (lib for a 32-bit binary), that old fixed value is searched next, so a library found there before still resolves. ld.so does not search that old value, so pack prints a note on stderr for a library found only there: at run time, only the image's ld.so.cache can find it. A string that holds :, tried whole, uses the glibc value only. With no such libc.so.6, the old value is the only one. Scratchsmith never scrapes the host's ldd, ld.so.cache, or LD_LIBRARY_PATH, so the result is deterministic.
  2. Stage: copy the interpreter to its verbatim path (another path to the loader becomes a relative symlink to that copy), mirror the libraries, recreate versioned-soname symlinks, regenerate ld.so.cache, and add the glibc NSS pieces. A musl binary gets no cache and no NSS (see The musl backend).
  3. Assemble: build a non-root image with reproducible layers (sorted entries, zeroed mtime/uid/gid). The uncompressed diff_id and the gzip layer digest are computed separately, which avoids the classic unpullable-image bug.

docs.title: The musl backend
docs.text:
The binary's program interpreter (PT_INTERP) picks the rules. A loader named ld-musl-* selects musl's rules for the whole graph, and any other loader selects the glibc rules above, which do not change. The musl backend supports x86_64 only, and a musl binary for any other architecture fails the pack. musl's loader (1.2.5) differs from glibc's in these ways, and Scratchsmith copies each one:

  1. No cache. musl has no ld.so.cache and no ldconfig, so pack writes neither and never runs ldconfig. musl opens a library only at the path its search found. When that path is a link into another directory, or passes through a directory link, the image gets a link at that path to the staged file.
  2. libc is the loader. A needed name of lib plus c., pthread., rt., m., dl., util. or xnet., such as libc.so, libc.musl-x86_64.so.1 or libm.so, is the loader itself, found with no search. So is a name equal to the PT_INTERP string.
  3. Search order. A name with no / matches an object already loaded under that name first. Then come the search path of the object that needs it, of the object that needed that one, and so on up to the program, then the system path.
  4. RPATH and RUNPATH are one value. RUNPATH wins when both are set, and either one is inherited by every dependency below it.
  5. Only $ORIGIN expands. A search path that holds any other $ token, such as $LIB, is dropped whole for that object, and pack prints a note.
  6. The system path comes from <prefix>/etc/ld-musl-<arch>.path in the host root, split on : and on newlines. The prefix is the PT_INTERP path less its last two parts. With no such file, it is /lib:/usr/local/lib:/usr/lib. When a library came from a directory outside those defaults, the image gets its own path file that lists those directories and the defaults.
  7. "Already loaded" goes by file name. musl never reads DT_SONAME. A name matches an object found under the same file name, or the same file by device and inode.
  8. A glibc libc is not loaded. musl takes a library that defines __libc_start_main and stdin for its own libc. Scratchsmith fails the pack on a glibc libc in a musl graph, and maps a copy of musl's libc to the loader.
  9. No skip on class or machine. glibc skips a library file of another ELF class or machine and keeps searching. musl opens the first file of the needed name and fails to load it. Scratchsmith takes that file too, and warns.

musl has no NSS: it reads /etc/passwd, /etc/group, /etc/hosts and /etc/resolv.conf directly. A musl image always gets the minimal /etc/passwd and /etc/group, and no nsswitch.conf or NSS module. One image has one libc, so an --add-binary program or library of the other libc fails the pack.

docs.title: Stability
docs.text:
Scratchsmith follows Semantic Versioning. As of 1.0, these surfaces are a stable contract. A breaking change to any of them requires a new major version:

  • CLI flags: the names and meaning of pack / lint / doctor / index / graph / diff / unpack / verify flags, and the top-level --completions and --verbose. New flags arrive in minor releases. A removed or renamed flag, or a changed default, is a major change.
  • scratchsmith.toml: the configuration keys and their types (the Configuration reference).
  • --format json: the field names and types of the pack, index, verify, graph, diff, unpack, and lint reports (the schema CI gates consume). Each is pinned by a golden test, so a change is always deliberate.
  • Exit codes: 0 on success. 2 on a usage error: an argument-parse error, or a command line that scratchsmith refuses after the parse, such as --watch --format json or pack with no binary. 1 on any other failure, such as a failed pack. Before 2.0.0, a refusal made after the parse exited 1. For scratchsmith.toml the same rule holds. A value that parses and is then refused exits 2, for example a label with no =. A file that cannot be read or parsed exits 1, for example a value of the wrong type or an unknown key. A nested [profile.a.profile.b] table is refused when the file loads, so it exits 1 too.

Not frozen (these can change in any release): human-readable text and warning wording, log output, doctor's exact phrasing, the Rust library API, and the exact bytes of the produced image. The crate's pub items exist for its own tests, not as a supported API. Layers stay reproducible for identical inputs, but that is a property, not a frozen API.

COMPATIBILITY.md covers how the contract changes over time. It describes the deprecation cycle (keep it working, warn on stderr, remove only in the next major), and how a test guards each surface.

docs.title: How Scratchsmith compares
docs.text:
Every tool here builds smaller and safer images. They differ mainly in what you feed them.

Input No Dockerfile Prebuilt dynamic glibc or musl binaries Built-in SBOM + hardening Daemonless build Scratchsmith a prebuilt dynamic ELF binary ✅ ✅ (the whole point; musl on x86_64) ✅ SBOM (via syft) + built-in ELF hardening lint ✅ --push / --oci-archive (the default sink uses docker load) Static + FROM scratch source you can static-link ✅ (COPY) ❌ must be static ❌ ✅ Docker multi-stage a Dockerfile + source ❌ ✅ (you hand-craft it) ❌ ❌ needs daemon / BuildKit apko apk packages ✅ ❌ needs apk packaging ✅ ✅ ko Go source ✅ ❌ Go only partial ✅ slim an already-built image ✅ ✅ (minifies) security profiles ❌ needs a built image first

Scratchsmith owns the one input the others do not serve: an arbitrary prebuilt dynamic binary.

Snapshot as of 2026-08. The other tools evolve, so read their own docs for current behavior. Only Scratchsmith's row is kept current here.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• glibc and musl, host arch only (for now). A dynamic glibc binary resolves by ld.so's rules. A dynamic musl binary resolves by musl's own loader rules, on x86_64 only. A musl binary for another arch is rejected with a clear error before anything is staged, so you never get a silently broken image. musl has no NSS and reads no glibc locales, so --nss and --locale are refused for it. (A static binary of either libc is a single self-contained file and packs fine.) No cross-arch resolution yet.
  • dlopen is best-effort. Libraries loaded at runtime via dlopen are invisible to static analysis. Scratchsmith warns about a dlopen reference in the binary's dynamic symbol table, and it lets you force-stage those libraries with --include <lib>. It is not a blanket "any binary just works" guarantee.
  • Loading into a container engine is the default sink. The default hands the image to a local engine for convenience: docker by default, or --runtime podman|nerdctl for those. You can also go daemon-free entirely with --push <ref> (straight to a registry), --oci-archive <file> (an OCI archive), or --no-build --output (a rootfs).
  • Signing the image pack produces needs a push target (--push or push in the config). pack --push --sign cosign-signs the pushed image by digest (keyless). --sbom --sign attaches the SBOM as a signed attestation. Both apply only to the registry-push sink, because cosign signs a registry image. Release artifacts are separately cosign-signed with SLSA provenance (Verifying releases).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Instead of a long command line, put the defaults for pack in a scratchsmith.toml and load it with --config. Every key below maps to a pack flag, and a command-line flag overrides the file.

scratchsmith.toml key CLI flag What it does binary (positional arg) The ELF binary to pack. entrypoint --entrypoint Image ENTRYPOINT (defaults to the packed binary's path). The binary keeps its real host path in the image, so an entrypoint that runs it must name that path. cmd --cmd Default arguments appended to the entrypoint (list, and --cmd is repeatable). env --env Image environment entries, each KEY=VALUE (list). An entry with no = fails the pack with exit code 2. Write KEY= for an empty value. workdir --workdir Image WORKDIR. user --user Image user UID[:GID]. Defaults to a non-root UID. 0/root prints a warning. label --label OCI image label KEY=VALUE (list, and --label is repeatable). An entry with no = fails the pack with exit code 2. Write KEY= for an empty value. healthcheck --healthcheck Container HEALTHCHECK in exec form (list, and repeatable). It runs inside the scratch image, so it must name an executable present there, typically the packed binary. strip --strip Strip symbols from the binary and libraries. A non-ELF --include file ships unchanged. upx --upx Compress the packed binary with UPX (it self-decompresses at runtime). smoke --smoke Run the built image once. If the binary cannot start, the pack fails. Needs the default load sink: with push, --oci-archive or --no-build it fails with exit code 2. sbom --sbom Write an SBOM of the packed rootfs (requires syft). sbom-file --sbom-file SBOM output path (default: sbom.json). Without sbom it is ignored, and the report warns. sbom-format --sbom-format SBOM format: cyclonedx-json (default) or spdx-json. Without sbom it is ignored, and the report warns. scan --scan Vulnerability-scan the packed rootfs with grype. When --sbom is set, it reuses that SBOM. Otherwise it scans the rootfs. scan-fail-on --scan-fail-on Fail the pack on a grype finding at or above this severity: negligible/low/medium/high/critical (implies --scan). negligible blocks everything, including findings grype cannot rank. Stricter levels ignore unrankable findings. ca-certs --ca-certs Add the TLS CA bundle (/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt, linked from /etc/ssl/cert.pem). tz --tz Add the resolved local timezone (/etc/localtime). tmp --tmp Add an empty /tmp directory, mode 1777 and owned by uid 0, so the non-root user can write there. A --no-build rootfs keeps the mode, owned by the user who packed it. init --init Add a minimal init (tini) as pid 1 wrapping the entrypoint. A static tini-static is preferred. A dynamic tini still packs, with a warning. add-file --add-file Copy a host file into the image (list). Each entry is SRC:DST, or a bare absolute SRC to keep the host path. With the default symlinks = "copy-all" the entry takes regular files only. A missing source, a directory, or a DST already in the image then fails the pack. Another symlinks mode changes that for a source that is itself a symlink. In an image the file lands owned by uid 0 at mode 0644, or 0755 for an executable source. The layer writer canonicalizes modes, so do not add a secret this way. add-binary --add-binary Copy a host ELF into the image with the shared libraries it needs (list, same SRC:DST or SRC form as add-file). Its libraries are resolved with the packed binary's loader rules (glibc's or musl's) and staged once. An ELF for another architecture, a program for another loader, or a program or library that uses the other libc fails the pack, and so does one that uses $ORIGIN with a DST outside its real directory. See Usage. locale --locale Stage a compiled glibc locale under /usr/lib/locale (list). Name it as glibc does, such as en_US.UTF-8. The data comes from a matching host directory under /usr/lib/locale. When there is none, localedef compiles the locale from /usr/share/i18n. The host locale-archive is never copied. Set LANG, LC_ALL, or a per-category LC_* entry with --env to select the locale. If nothing selects a staged locale, the pack warns. If a selector names a locale the pack did not stage, the pack warns as well. glibc only: set for a musl binary, it fails the pack with exit 2. symlinks --symlinks What a symlink you name becomes in the image: copy-all (default), preserve, copy-unsafe, or skip-unsafe. Covers the packed binary path and each add-file source. See Usage for the mode table. include --include Force-stage extra libraries by soname or path, for example dlopen'd plugins (list). nss --nss Name-service (NSS) modules to stage for glibc name lookups: files, dns, or none (list). Fewer modules trim CVE surface. A mode without files also drops /etc/passwd and /etc/group, which glibc reads through the files module. Default: files and dns. glibc only: set for a musl binary, it fails the pack with exit 2. packages --packages Where to record the distribution packages that own the bundled files: report, sbom, image, or none (list). Default: report,sbom (report before 2.0, see Deprecations). With the text report and no value set, scratchsmith drops report. sbom shows the packages to --sbom and --scan. If neither is on, sbom does nothing. A sbom you set then warns, and the default stays quiet. image adds package records and /etc/os-release to the image. Needs a dpkg or rpm host. On another host, image you set fails the pack. If --sbom or --scan is on, a sbom you set fails the pack too. The default stays quiet there. deny --deny If this library ships, the pack fails (list). Resolved libraries, the loader, and NSS modules are all in scope, matched by soname or staged file name. This is a CI policy gate. Read library sonames from scratchsmith graph. It does not list the NSS modules. require --require If this library does not ship, the pack fails (list). Same scope as deny. sign --sign cosign-sign the pushed image (keyless, by digest). Requires a push target. push-untagged --push-untagged Push the image by its digest only, creating or moving no image tag (sign still adds cosign's sha256-<hex> signature tags). The push reference then names just the repository. Needs a push target, like sign. See Usage. push --push Push the image straight to this registry reference, daemonless. A sink on the command line (--push, --oci-archive or --no-build) replaces this key. If the file also sets sign, --oci-archive or --no-build leaves it no push target, and the pack fails with exit code 2. max-size --max-size If the packed image exceeds this size, the pack fails. The packed image is the fully-staged rootfs: payload + NSS includes + runtime extras + added files + locales + the --packages image records. Write the size as 12MB, 512KiB, or a bare byte count (K/M/G are ×1000, Ki/Mi/Gi are ×1024). runtime --runtime Container engine for the default load sink and the --smoke run: docker (default), podman, or nerdctl. The daemonless sinks (--oci-archive, --push) never invoke a runtime, so this is ignored there.

A key that is not in this table, or a value of the wrong type, fails the pack with exit code 1. A relative path in the file is read from the directory where you run scratchsmith, not from the directory of the file.

A full config file, and how to run it:

# scratchsmith.toml — loaded with `scratchsmith pack --config scratchsmith.toml`.
binary = "/opt/app/bin/app"
entrypoint = "/opt/app/bin/app"   # the default; the binary keeps its host path in the image
cmd = ["--serve"]
env = ["LANG=C.UTF-8"]
workdir = "/data"
user = "65532:65532"
label = ["role=api"]
healthcheck = ["/opt/app/bin/app", "--health"]
strip = true
upx = true
# smoke = true                 # needs the default load sink, so it cannot go with `push`
sbom = true
sbom-file = "sbom.json"
sbom-format = "cyclonedx-json"
scan = true
scan-fail-on = "high"
ca-certs = true
tz = true
tmp = true
init = true
add-file = ["./app.conf:/etc/app/app.conf", "/etc/motd"]
add-binary = ["/usr/bin/bash:/bin/bash"]
locale = ["en_US.UTF-8"]
symlinks = "copy-all"
include = ["libnss_myhostname.so.2"]
nss = ["files", "dns"]
packages = ["report", "sbom"]
deny = ["libssl.so.3"]
require = ["libseccomp.so.2"]
sign = true
push = "ghcr.io/you/app:latest"
# push-untagged = true        # needs a `push` reference with no tag, so not this one
max-size = "50MB"
runtime = "docker"

scratchsmith pack --config scratchsmith.toml                 # binary + all keys come from the file
scratchsmith pack --config scratchsmith.toml --push ghcr.io/you/app:dev ./other   # CLI overrides binary + push

The delivery sinks --oci-archive <file> and --no-build / --output <dir>, the display-only --format, and --watch stay command-line-only. They are not config keys.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
Group keys under [profile.<name>] and pick one with --profile <name> (which requires --config). A profile layers over the base config, so shared keys live at the top level and per-environment overrides go in the profile:

binary = "./dist/app"
strip = true

[profile.ci]                    # scratchsmith pack --config scratchsmith.toml --profile ci
sbom = true
sign = true
push = "ghcr.io/you/app:latest"

Values layer in this order, last wins: base config → the selected [profile.<name>] → any command-line flag. Booleans OR together, so a profile or a flag can switch something on but not off. To switch it off, remove the key from the file. A scalar is replaced by the more specific layer. A non-empty list replaces the one beneath it.

Profiles do not nest. A table such as [profile.a.profile.b] fails the pack with exit code 1, and the error names each nested table by its full path. Move each one to a top-level [profile.<name>] table. See Deprecations.

docs.title: Deprecations
docs.text:
Scratchsmith keeps its contract in COMPATIBILITY.md. Only a major version can change it, and nothing on it disappears without notice. This page lists everything on the way out, and what you write instead.

This page has one list for each kind of change. Two kinds change only in a major version: deprecated input shapes and tolerances. Refused input is a third kind, because a minor release can refuse input that is the attack itself. The last list, Removed in 2.0.0, shows what version 2.0.0 changed after its deprecation cycle ended. Most inputs there now fail, and one gets a new default. It also shows five changes in 2.0.0 with no warning first:

  • an exit code
  • an output directory that cannot be listed
  • an --include file that is not a regular file
  • a program or a library at a package record path
  • a DT_NEEDED library in a directory whose name holds :

A deprecated input shape still works. Scratchsmith accepts it, prints one warning line to standard error, and exits with the same code as before. The next major version refuses it.

A tolerance is different. Scratchsmith accepts input today that it cannot use in full, and the result can be an image with a part absent. The next major version reports it as an error. Each tolerance prints one warning line to standard error, and the exit code stays the same.

docs.title: Deprecated input shapes
docs.text:
Version 2.0.0 removed the 1.x deprecations, and the list Removed in 2.0.0 names each one.

Input Warned since In 3.0 Write this instead A digest in the --push reference (or the push key), such as ghcr.io/owner/app@sha256:… 2.1.0 Refused A tag, such as ghcr.io/owner/app:1.0, or the repository alone with --push-untagged A diff argument that is not a directory, such as diff a.tar b.tar 2.1.0 Refused Two rootfs directories, such as from pack --no-build --output or unpack

A registry stores a manifest only under that manifest's own digest. A push to any other digest fails at the registry, and nobody knows the right digest before the image is built. With --sign, scratchsmith already signs the image by the digest that the push stored. Through 2.0.3, a push to a digest could also crash scratchsmith when the registry answered without a Location header, as AWS ECR does. That crash is fixed, and the push still goes to the digest.

diff compares two directory trees. It reads a file argument as an empty tree, so diff --exit-code a.tar b.tar prints no changes and exits 0 for two different archives. Through 2.0.3 it did so with no warning. To compare two OCI archives, unpack each one into a directory and compare those.

docs.title: Refused without a deprecation cycle
docs.text: Some input was the attack itself. COMPATIBILITY.md allows a minor or patch release to refuse such input with no deprecation cycle, and this section lists each case.

docs.title: A library that is not a regular file
docs.text:
A DT_NEEDED name can resolve to a FIFO, a device, or a socket. Through 1.7.2, the read of a FIFO waited forever for a writer, or read a writer's stream with no end. Now pack and graph refuse such a library before they open it, and exit 1. No library is a FIFO, so no working image depends on one.

A FIFO that you name with --include is still read, so graph --include <(cat libplugin.so) works. pack reads it too, but then it refuses to stage it, because it is not a regular file, and exits 1. Both commands open the FIFO and wait for a writer, as cat does. With no writer they wait until you stop them, and that is accepted behavior.

docs.title: A file that is not an ELF, named by the binary or a library
docs.text:
A DT_NEEDED entry in the binary or in a library names a file. The binary's program interpreter (PT_INTERP) names a file too. Through 1.7.2, scratchsmith staged that file, and it did not check that the file was an ELF. The name can point at any file on the host, such as ~/.docker/config.json, and that file shipped in the image.

Now pack and graph refuse such a file and exit 1. The loader cannot start a binary that needs it, so no working image depends on it. A data file that you name with --include still stages. A library deeper in the tree that names the same file then resolves to that staged copy.

docs.title: An ELF that the loader cannot load, named by the binary or a library
docs.text:
The same names can point at a host file that is an ELF but not a library, such as a core dump. Through 1.7.2, scratchsmith staged that file. A core dump holds the memory of a crashed process, which can include secrets.

Now pack and graph refuse such a file and exit 1. A library must be a shared object (ET_DYN). glibc refuses any other type with "cannot dynamically load executable", so no working image depends on one. A program interpreter must be ET_DYN or ET_EXEC, because the kernel loads both.

This check reads the ELF type only. A PIE executable is ET_DYN too, so a name that points at one still stages it. A core dump, an object file (ET_REL), and an executable built without PIE do not. A file that you name with --include stages as before. If the binary itself also names that file, the refusal comes first.

docs.title: An archive entry or a piped archive with no size limit
docs.text:
unpack holds every blob of an image archive in memory. Through 1.7.2, a large or sparse archive file let one entry fill memory, and an archive read from a pipe had no total limit.

Now unpack refuses an entry larger than 2 GiB plus 2 MiB, and a pipe that yields more than 16 GiB in all, and exits 1. A gzip layer that decompresses past 2 GiB was already refused, so an uncompressed layer over 2 GiB is now refused too. An archive file on disk keeps its own size as the total limit.

There is no way around this limit. unpack cannot read a layer over 2 GiB of either type, and gzipping the layer does not help, because a gzip layer stops at the same limit.

docs.title: A gzip layer of more than one member
docs.text:
A gzip layer can hold several gzip members, one after another, as cat a.gz b.gz writes. Docker reads every member. Through 2.0.0, unpack read only the first, so a second member could carry files that the image installs and the audit never showed.

Now unpack reads every member. Bytes after the last member that do not start another member make unpack fail with exit 1. Docker refuses those bytes too, so no working image has them.

docs.title: A layer with data after its end, or cut short
docs.text:
A layer's tar ends with a block of zeros. Through 2.0.0, unpack stopped there and ignored what followed. A reader that skips zero blocks would find entries hidden after it. unpack also deleted a lower layer's files for a layer's whiteouts before it found that the layer was cut short.

Now unpack refuses a layer with any byte other than zero after that block, and exits 1. Zeros there are only padding, and still pass. A layer cut short inside an entry fails before unpack writes or deletes any file for that layer. The layers before it are already applied.

docs.title: A sparse entry in a layer
docs.text:
A sparse tar entry stores only part of a file, and the reader fills the holes with zeros. A few header bytes can then claim a file of any size, and fill the disk. Through 2.0.0, unpack wrote such an entry from a layer. It already refused one in the outer archive.

Now unpack refuses a sparse entry in a layer, in GNU or PAX form, and exits 1. It refuses the layer before it writes any file from it. Docker and BuildKit write layers with Go's tar library, which cannot write a sparse entry, so no working image has one.

docs.title: A malformed PAX record in a layer
docs.text:
A PAX record is a line in a tar header that holds extra details for the next entry, such as a long name. Through 2.0.0, unpack skipped a record that it could not parse, and wrote the entry anyway.

Now unpack refuses a layer with a malformed PAX record, and exits 1. It refuses the layer before it writes any file from it, and the error names the entry. Docker's tar reader refuses such a record too, so no working image has one.

docs.title: An image whose layers decompress past 16 GiB in all
docs.text:
Each layer stops at 2 GiB once decompressed, but a manifest can list the same layer many times. Through 2.0.1, one small gzip layer listed N times decompressed N times, and unpack wrote up to N times 2 GiB to the target.

Now unpack refuses an image whose layers hold more than 16 GiB in all once decompressed, and exits 1. A layer listed twice counts twice, and an uncompressed layer counts at its own size. The error names the limit. The layers before the one that crosses it are already applied.

docs.title: A whiteout that climbs above the image root
docs.text:
A whiteout marker is a layer entry named .wh.<name>, which deletes <name> from the layers below. Through 2.0.2, unpack skipped a marker whose path had a .. part, and applied the rest of the layer. That missed a marker like etc/../etc/.wh.keep, which Docker cleans to etc/.wh.keep and honors, so the unpacked tree kept a file that the image deletes.

Now unpack cleans the marker's path as Docker does, and deletes what it names. A rooted path stops at /, so /../etc/.wh.keep deletes etc/keep. A relative path whose .. climbs above the root, such as ../.wh.x, makes unpack refuse the layer and exit 1. It refuses the layer before it writes or deletes any file for it. Docker refuses that marker too, so no working image has one.

docs.title: An OCI archive with two index.json files
docs.text:
An OCI archive holds one index.json, which names the image. A tar file can still hold two entries with that name, or index.json and ./index.json. Through 2.0.2, unpack kept the last one and said nothing. Another tool that keeps the first would show a different image from the same archive.

Now unpack refuses the archive and exits 1. The error names the second entry as it is stored. It refuses before it reads that entry. No OCI layout writer puts two index.json files in one archive, so no working image has one.

docs.title: An identity token sent to an http realm, or across a redirect
docs.text:
A Docker config can hold a login as an identity token, a refresh token that --push and index exchange for an access token at the realm that the registry names. Through 2.0.2, the exchange posted the refresh token to that realm over plain http too, and followed a redirect from it with the token in the body. A registry, or anyone on the network path, could then read the refresh token.

Now the realm must be https, and a redirect from it is refused, not followed. Either one makes --push or index fail with exit 1. The one exception is an http realm on a loopback address, for a registry at localhost, 127.0.0.1 or ::1, which scratchsmith already reaches over http. Hosted registries such as Docker Hub and GHCR name an https realm, and a local test registry keeps working, so no working push depends on the refused realm.

docs.title: Tolerances ending in 2.0
docs.text: No tolerance is left now. Version 2.0.0 ended the 1.x tolerances, and the list Removed in 2.0.0 names each one.

docs.title: Removed in 2.0.0
