A script that tests for exactly 1 must also accept 2 --packages (the packages key) with no value 1.9.0 The default is report,sbom, so --sbom and --scan see the packages and a --scan-fail-on gate can find more --packages report (or packages = ["report"]) for the 1.x result pack --no-build --output DIR into a DIR that is not empty 1.6.0 An error before any file is staged. pack exits 1 A new or empty directory, or rm -rf DIR first pack --no-build --output DIR into a DIR that cannot be listed Not warned An error. pack exits 1 A directory that you can read, or a new one $PLATFORM in a search path, on an architecture with no value for it 1.6.0 An error. pack and graph exit 1 and name the file that holds the search path Write the directory name in the path A program interpreter (PT_INTERP) that starts like an ELF and cannot be parsed 1.8.0 An error. pack and graph exit 1 and name the file Replace the damaged loader with an intact copy The program or an --include library at a package record path on the host. This applies to an explicit image in --packages, or an explicit sbom with --sbom or --scan Not warned An error. pack exits 1 and names the path. 1.x exited 0, and the record replaced the file Remove sbom and image from --packages, or move the file on the host A DT_NEEDED library only in a directory whose name holds :, which ldconfig does not cache Not warned Missing. pack and graph exit 1, and a note: line names the directory. 1.x exited 0, and the image exited 127 at start. An --include file there still stages Move the library to a directory with no : in its name

docs.title: A library found only through an inherited RPATH
docs.text:
An RPATH is inherited: a library that the program loads also searches the program's RPATH. A library that has its own RUNPATH does not search any inherited RPATH for the libraries that it needs. Scratchsmith now applies that rule with no fallback, so the library is missing, as it is for the loader. A note: line on stderr names the directory and the library that needs the file. To fix it, link the library that needs the file with a RUNPATH that holds the directory:

$ cc -shared -fPIC -Wl,--enable-new-dtags -Wl,-rpath,/opt/app/lib -o libmid.so mid.c -lleaf

docs.title: A command line refused after the parse exits 2
docs.text: Scratchsmith refuses some command lines only after the parse, because the refusal needs a second flag or the config. Examples are --watch --format json, pack with no binary, and one --add-file image path given twice. In 1.x these refusals exited 1, the code for a failed pack, and printed no warning about a change. In 2.0.0 they exit 2, the same code as an argument-parse error. This change had no deprecation cycle, because the 1.x contract promised only a non-zero code for these refusals. A script that tests for exactly 1 must also accept 2.

docs.title: An output directory that cannot be listed
docs.text: pack --no-build --output DIR checks that DIR is empty. In 1.x the check skipped a DIR that it had no permission to list, so it printed no warning and packed into it. Version 2.0.0 refuses that DIR, because it cannot prove that the directory is empty. This change had no warning before 2.0. Give the pack a directory that you can read, or a new one.

docs.title: $PLATFORM with no value
docs.text:
A library search path is an RPATH or a RUNPATH entry in the binary, or in a library that the binary needs. It can contain the token $PLATFORM, and the loader replaces that token with the name of the processor type. Scratchsmith knows that name for x86_64 and aarch64 only.

On any other architecture, the token has no value. Through 1.9, scratchsmith removed the token and searched what was left, so /opt/app/lib/$PLATFORM became the parent directory /opt/app/lib/. A library with the same name in that directory then shipped in place of the correct one. Now pack and graph stop with exit 1 where 1.x warned, and the error names the file that holds the search path. A search path that the loader never reads still passes, for example an RPATH in a file that also has RUNPATH. When you link that file, write the directory name in the search path and do not use the token:

$ cc -Wl,-rpath,/opt/app/lib/riscv64 -o myapp main.c

docs.title: GitHub Action
docs.text:
Pack in CI with no shell glue. The composite action downloads the signed release binary for the runner, verifies it against the release checksums, and runs pack:

- uses: schubydoo/scratchsmith@v<ver>   # pin to a release tag
  with:
    binary: ./dist/app         # your prebuilt dynamic glibc or musl binary
    sbom: true                 # needs syft on the runner
    strip: true
    smoke: true                # fail the job if the packed image can't start

A musl binary (x86_64 only) packs the same way, but pack reads its libraries from the runner, so the runner needs musl's loader at /lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1. On an Ubuntu runner, install the musl package in an earlier step. See Pack a musl binary. musl needs scratchsmith v2.3.0 or later.

To publish the built image, log in first and set push:

- uses: docker/login-action@v4
  with:
    registry: ghcr.io
    username: ${{ github.actor }}
    password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}   # the job needs `permissions: packages: write`
- uses: schubydoo/scratchsmith@v<ver>   # pin to a release tag
  with:
    binary: ./dist/app
    push: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest   # must be lowercase: spell it out if the name has capitals

Ten inputs take one value per line: cmd, env, label, healthcheck, add-file, add-binary, locale, include, deny, and require. Set image metadata, gate on vulnerabilities, or cap the size:

- uses: schubydoo/scratchsmith@v<ver>
  with:
    binary: ./dist/app
    env: |
      LANG=C.UTF-8
    workdir: /data
    label: |
      org.opencontainers.image.source=https://github.com/you/app
      role=api
    healthcheck: |
      ${{ github.workspace }}/dist/app
      --health
    scan: true
    scan-fail-on: high        # needs grype on the runner
    max-size: 25MB

The binary is staged at its real absolute path on the runner, and that path is also the default entrypoint. So a healthcheck or entrypoint has to name that path, not a short one like /app.

Pin @v<ver> to a specific release tag (or a commit SHA). That is the same supply-chain hygiene the tool itself practices. version: overrides which scratchsmith release the action runs (defaults to the pinned tag, else latest). The action only reads a version from a vX.Y.Z tag ref, so if you pin a commit SHA, also set version: to the matching release (for example version: v2.2.0). Otherwise a SHA pin downloads the latest release.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Most inputs map to the pack flag of the same name. See Configuration for what each does, and Usage for the equivalent command-line recipes. A few inputs are action-specific. version picks which release to download. output maps to --no-build --output. args is split on whitespace and appended to the command. Quotes are not honoured, so a value cannot hold a space, and an unquoted * or ? expands against the workspace. It is the escape hatch for any flag without a dedicated input, for example --oci-archive out.tar, or --push <ref> --sign for a daemonless, cosign-signed push (that job needs permissions: id-token: write). With --push or --oci-archive in args, the image output is empty, because only the default docker-load sink sets it. Note that push publishes with docker tag/docker push, not pack's daemonless, cosign-signable --push.

The action reads the JSON report, so every pack through it runs the --packages lookup by default. The report output holds a packages list and a timings object. To turn the lookup off, set the packages input to none.

Input Default Description binary (required) Path to the dynamically linked ELF binary to pack (glibc, or musl on x86_64). version (the pinned tag, else latest) Which scratchsmith release to download: a tag like v1.0.0, or latest. output Stage the rootfs into this directory instead of building an image (--no-build). The directory must be new or empty. entrypoint (the binary's path) Image ENTRYPOINT. cmd Default arguments appended to the entrypoint, one per line. env Image environment entries, one KEY=VALUE per line. A line with no = fails the pack. Write KEY= for an empty value. workdir Image WORKDIR. user 65532 Image user UID[:GID]. 0 warns. label OCI image labels, one KEY=VALUE per line. A line with no = fails the pack. Write KEY= for an empty value. healthcheck HEALTHCHECK in exec form, one token per line. It must name an executable in the image. strip false Strip symbols from the binary and libraries. upx false Compress the binary with UPX (needs upx on the runner). smoke false After the build, run the image once. If the binary cannot start, the job fails. It cannot be combined with output, because output builds no image. sbom false Generate an SBOM of the packed rootfs (needs syft on the runner). sbom-file sbom.json SBOM output path. Requires sbom, and is ignored on its own. sbom-format cyclonedx-json SBOM format: cyclonedx-json or spdx-json. scan false Vulnerability-scan the rootfs with grype (needs grype on the runner). When sbom is set, it reuses that SBOM. scan-fail-on Fail on a grype finding at or above this severity (negligible…critical). Implies scan. ca-certs false Add the TLS CA bundle to the image. tz false Add the resolved local timezone to the image. init false Add a minimal init (tini) as pid 1 wrapping the entrypoint. tmp false Add an empty, writable /tmp (mode 1777, owned by uid 0), so the non-root user can write there with no --tmpfs mount. See Usage. Needs scratchsmith v2.1.0 or later. add-file Copy host files into the image, one SRC:DST per line. A bare absolute SRC keeps its own path. Regular files only, and a missing source, a directory, or a DST already in the image fails the pack. A symlinks mode that stages a link changes two of those rules for a symlink source. A preserved link is staged as a link, so a link to a directory no longer fails. Under skip-unsafe, an entry the pack cannot honor stages nothing and warns. A taken DST still fails under every mode. The file lands owned by uid 0 at mode 0644, or 0755 for an executable source, so do not add a secret this way. add-binary Copy host ELF programs into the image with the shared libraries they need, one SRC:DST per line. A bare absolute SRC keeps its own path. Each program's libraries resolve by the same loader rules as the packed binary, and a library both need is staged once. An ELF for another architecture, a program for another loader, or a program or library that uses the other libc fails the pack, and so does one that uses $ORIGIN with a DST outside its real directory. A path may hold spaces, which args cannot pass. See Usage. Needs scratchsmith v2.1.0 or later. locale Compiled glibc locales to stage at /usr/lib/locale, one name per line, for example en_US.UTF-8. A name, never a path. Needs a prebuilt directory on the runner, or localedef plus the glibc sources at /usr/share/i18n. Staging a locale does not select it, so also set LANG through env. The host locale-archive is never copied. glibc only: set for a musl binary, it fails the pack. symlinks copy-all What a symlink you name becomes in the image: copy-all, preserve, copy-unsafe, or skip-unsafe. Covers the packed binary's own path and each add-file source, never the resolved libraries. include Extra libraries to force-stage, for example dlopen'd plugins, one soname/path per line. nss files,dns NSS modules to stage for glibc lookups, comma-separated (files,dns, or none). Fewer modules trim CVE surface. glibc only: set for a musl binary, it fails the pack. packages report,sbom Where to record the distribution packages that own the bundled files, comma-separated: report, sbom, image, or none. sbom shows them to sbom and scan. image keeps the package records in the image. A sbom you set does nothing, and warns, unless the sbom or the scan input is on. The default sbom stays quiet. With a 1.x version, the default is report. Set report to keep the 1.x result. See Usage. max-size If the fully-staged image exceeds this size, the job fails. Write the size as 25MB, 512KiB, or a byte count. deny If a listed library ships, fail the pack (soname or staged file name), one per line. require If a listed library does not ship, fail the pack (same scope as deny), one per line. push Tag the built image as this registry ref and docker push it. Needs a prior registry login. Not compatible with output. args Extra raw pack flags, split on whitespace (no quoting) and appended: the escape hatch for anything above.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: Output Description image The loaded image tag. It is empty when output staged a rootfs, or when --push or --oci-archive in args replaced the docker load. rootfs The staged rootfs directory. When an image was built instead, this is empty. report The full pack report as JSON.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Scratchsmith is Linux only (amd64/arm64). It stages a Linux rootfs, so it does not run on macOS or native Windows. Use a Linux container or WSL2 there.

docs.title: One-line install
docs.text:
Downloads the signed release binary, verifies it against the cosign-signed checksums.txt, and installs it to ~/.local/bin (or /usr/local/bin as root):

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/schubydoo/scratchsmith/main/install.sh | bash

Piping to bash runs install.sh. You can read it first. The VERSION and BIN_DIR env vars override the tag and install directory. VERSION takes the tag with or without its leading v, for example curl -fsSL …/install.sh | VERSION=v2.2.0 bash. Without cosign, the script warns and verifies only the SHA-256. With cosign installed, a missing signature bundle stops the install. The INSECURE_ALLOW_MISSING_SIGNATURE=1 env var installs anyway and verifies only the SHA-256. A signature that fails to verify still stops the install. If a download stalls for 30 seconds, the script stops with an error. It does not retry. That limit needs curl, or a wget that takes -T. A BusyBox wget that was built with no timeout feature can still hang. Uninstall with --uninstall:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/schubydoo/scratchsmith/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --uninstall

docs.title: Homebrew
docs.text: brew install schubydoo/scratchsmith/scratchsmith

docs.title: Cargo
docs.text:
Build and install from source with Cargo (Rust 1.96+):

cargo install --locked scratchsmith

--locked builds with the dependency versions the release was tested with. Without it, Cargo resolves the dependencies fresh and can pick crates that need a newer Rust than 1.96.

docs.title: Release binary
docs.text:
Download a release binary, Linux amd64 or arm64, from the latest release. Verify the signature and provenance first (see Verifying releases):

tar -xzf scratchsmith-*-linux-amd64.tar.gz   # or -linux-arm64
./scratchsmith-*/scratchsmith --version

docs.title: Container image
docs.text:
Pull the signed image:

docker pull ghcr.io/schubydoo/scratchsmith:latest

:latest is a minimal FROM scratch image. It runs every subcommand that needs no external tool, index included. It does not run pack, because a scratch image carries none of the tools pack needs. To run pack inside a container, pull the :toolbox image instead (Wolfi base + the full toolchain). The toolbox section in Usage lists which subcommands run where.

To pin a release, use :X.Y.Z or :X.Y (for example :2.2.0 or :2.2). The toolbox equivalents are :X.Y.Z-toolbox and :X.Y-toolbox. There is no major-only tag. Both images are multi-arch (amd64 and arm64) and signed. Verify them with the cosign verify command in Verifying releases.

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text:
Rust 1.96+:

git clone https://github.com/schubydoo/scratchsmith
cd scratchsmith
cargo build --release
# binary at target/release/scratchsmith

Run scratchsmith doctor to see which optional external tools (syft, strip, tini, …) are present.

docs.title: Shell completions
docs.text:
Generate a script for your shell and drop it where the shell looks:

scratchsmith --completions bash | sudo tee /etc/bash_completion.d/scratchsmith
scratchsmith --completions zsh  > ~/.zfunc/_scratchsmith    # ensure ~/.zfunc is on $fpath
scratchsmith --completions fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/scratchsmith.fish

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Pack a dynamic binary into a scratch image and run it:

scratchsmith pack ./app
docker run --rm scratchsmith/app:packed --version   # image is scratchsmith/<name>:packed, <name> lowercased (other characters an image name cannot hold become -)

The image gets the build host's glibc (or, for a musl binary, its musl). A binary built against a newer glibc than the host's packs, and then fails to start with an error like version `GLIBC_2.38' not found. pack reads the GLIBC_ versions that the binary and each library need. For each object that needs a version the staged glibc does not define, it adds a warning to the report that names the highest missing version. The text report prints it on standard output as warning: …, and --format json lists it in warnings. The pack still succeeds, with the same exit code. Pack on a host whose glibc is as new as the one the binary was built against.

The default sink loads into Docker. To load with podman or nerdctl instead (and run --smoke with it), pass --runtime:

scratchsmith pack --runtime podman ./app

Inspect the rootfs without building an image (no Docker daemon needed):

scratchsmith pack --no-build --output ./rootfs ./app    # or -n -o ./rootfs

Give --output a new directory or an empty one. Scratchsmith does not empty the directory, so a directory that holds anything is an error, and nothing is staged. A file is an error too. A directory that scratchsmith cannot list is an error, because it cannot prove the directory is empty. Remove the old directory first, or choose another. A pack that fails after it starts to stage, for example on --deny, leaves the partial tree in the directory. Remove the directory before you run the pack again.

Or write a daemonless OCI archive (loadable by skopeo/buildah, and pushable to a registry with no Docker daemon):

scratchsmith pack --oci-archive ./app.oci.tar ./app

For a regular file, scratchsmith writes the archive to a temporary file beside the target, and then renames it. A failed pack never leaves half an archive under the name that you gave. The directory of the archive must be writable. A pack that is interrupted can leave one .scratchsmith-oci-*.tmp file there, which is safe to delete.

A destination that already exists and is not a regular file is different. Examples are /dev/stdout, a FIFO and a symbolic link. Scratchsmith writes straight into it, with no temporary file and no rename.

Or push straight to a registry, with no Docker daemon. Credentials come from your Docker configuration, so docker login once (for GitHub's ghcr.io, a token with write:packages):

echo "$GHCR_TOKEN" | docker login ghcr.io -u YOUR_GH_USERNAME --password-stdin
scratchsmith pack --push ghcr.io/you/app:latest ./app

Add --sign to cosign-sign the pushed image by digest (keyless), and --sbom --sign to attach the SBOM as a signed attestation:

scratchsmith pack --push ghcr.io/you/app:latest --sbom --sign ./app

--sign checks that cosign runs before anything is pushed. It signs the digest of the manifest that scratchsmith sent, also when the registry's answer names no digest, and refuses one that names another digest. If signing fails after the push, the error says that the image was pushed but is not signed. index --sign works the same way.

A reference with no tag pushes to latest, as it always has. To push the image without creating or moving an image tag, add --push-untagged and name only the repository:

scratchsmith pack --push ghcr.io/you/app --push-untagged --sign ./app

The manifest goes up under its own digest. The report gives the pushed ghcr.io/you/app@sha256:... reference (the pushed field in --format json), and --sign signs that digest. cosign still stores the signature, and the SBOM attestation if there is one, under a sha256-<hex> tag in the same repository, so --sign adds those tags. No image tag is created or moved. A tag or a digest in the reference is a usage error with exit code 2. Tag the image later, for example after a review, with crane tag or oras tag.

cosign signs and attests with your terminal's standard input and standard error. Outside CI, keyless signing prints a login URL there and can ask for a code, and you answer it as you would when you run cosign yourself. cosign's standard output stays captured, so --format json stays parseable. A failed cosign run is reported with its exit status, and its own messages are above.

To check the signature later, against the signer you expect, run scratchsmith verify. See Verifying an image you signed with pack.

docs.title: Supply-chain output, smoke-run, and size gates
docs.text:
scratchsmith pack --sbom --strip --smoke ./app        # SBOM + stripped + auto smoke-run
scratchsmith pack --sbom --sbom-format spdx-json --sbom-file bom.spdx.json ./app   # SPDX SBOM, custom path
scratchsmith pack --scan --scan-fail-on high ./app    # grype vuln scan; fail the build on a high+ CVE
scratchsmith pack --strip --max-size 8MB ./app        # fail the build if the staged image exceeds 8 MB
scratchsmith lint --fail-on no-pie --fail-on no-relro ./app   # hardening gate for CI
scratchsmith lint --format json --fail-on no-fortify ./app     # the same report as JSON

lint --format json prints one object: binary (the path as given), hardening (pie, nx, canary and fortify as booleans, relro as "full", "partial" or "none"), fail_on (the gates asked for) and violations (the gates this binary fails). Gates use the --fail-on spelling, each listed once in the order given, so a CI script can feed a violation back to the flag. The report prints in full before a failing gate exits 1. The six gates are:

Gate Fails when no-pie the binary is not PIE no-relro it has no RELRO partial-relro its RELRO is not full (so it also fails with no RELRO) no-nx its stack is executable no-canary it imports no stack-protector guard no-fortify it imports no *_chk wrapper

canary and fortify mean the binary imports the guard or a *_chk wrapper, so a static binary reads false.

The report also carries libc ("glibc", "musl", or null for a binary with no loader) and fortify_detectable. musl's fortify-headers check in inline code and leave no *_chk symbol, so for a musl binary the text report shows Fortify: unknown (musl's fortify-headers leave no symbol), fortify is false and fortify_detectable is false. --fail-on no-fortify cannot be checked there, so it fails every musl binary: lint warns on standard error that the gate cannot be checked, prints the report and exits 1. The other gates work for musl as for glibc.

--smoke runs the image once and fails the pack only when the binary could not start: a missing library or loader, or an entrypoint the runtime could not exec. An app that starts and exits with an error passes, unless the code is 126 or 127, which shells use for a command that could not run. A binary still running after 15 seconds counts as started, and its container is removed. --smoke needs the default load sink: with --no-build, --oci-archive or --push (or a push key in the configuration file) it is a usage error, exit code 2.

syft, grype and cosign each have a time limit: syft 15 minutes, grype 30 minutes, and cosign 10 minutes. A run past its limit is stopped, and the pack fails with an error that names the tool and the limit. grype's limit leaves room for its first run, which downloads its vulnerability database.

--push and index give up on a registry or token host that does not accept the connection within 30 seconds, and the error names the endpoint. The identity-token exchange also fails after 60 seconds of silence from the token host. Talking to the registry itself has no read limit, so a slow upload of a large layer is not cut off, and a registry that accepts the connection and then sends nothing still keeps the command waiting.

A login stored as an identity token (identitytoken in the Docker config) is exchanged for an access token at the realm the registry names. scratchsmith sends it only to an https realm, or to a loopback http realm for a local registry, and follows no redirect from that realm. A failed exchange shows at most the first 1 KiB of the token host's answer, escaped.

The report names the loader the image carries, because the binary's PT_INTERP chooses that path and not scratchsmith. --format json carries it as interpreter, so a job can assert it without unpacking the image. An ELF that carries no PT_INTERP reports null, which is the case for a static binary.

scratchsmith pack --format json ./app | jq -e '.interpreter == "/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2"'

libc names the C library behind that loader: "glibc", "musl", or null with no loader.

--format json also carries timings: the time that each phase of the pack took, in milliseconds. Use it to find the slow part of a pack in CI, or to turn the phases into the spans of a build trace.

scratchsmith pack --format json --sbom --oci-archive app.tar ./app | jq .timings

{
  "resolve_ms": 19,
  "stage_ms": 9,
  "sbom_ms": 1569,
  "scan_ms": null,
  "deliver_ms": 734,
  "smoke_ms": null,
  "sign_ms": null,
  "total_ms": 2332
}
Field Phase resolve_ms Read the binary and resolve its libraries stage_ms Build the root filesystem: libraries, loader, NSS, extras, added files, locales, strip and UPX, and the package lookup sbom_ms Generate the SBOM (--sbom) scan_ms Scan for vulnerabilities (--scan) deliver_ms Build the image and load it, write the archive, or push it smoke_ms Smoke-run the image (--smoke) sign_ms Sign the image and attest the SBOM (--sign) total_ms The whole pack

A phase that did not run is null. With --no-build, deliver_ms is null, because no image is built. The phases add up to a little less than total_ms. The text report does not show the timings.

The other fields of the pack report:

  • tag, archive, pushed, staged_dir: where the image went. The one for the sink you used is set and the others are null: the loaded image tag, the --oci-archive path, the --push reference, or the --no-build directory.
  • entrypoint: the packed binary's path in the image. It does not change with --entrypoint or --init.
  • size: entries (each with path, before and after in bytes), total_before, total_after, and the booleans stripped and upx. It covers the ELF payload: the binary, the loader, the libraries and the NSS modules. An --add-binary program's libraries are included, and the added program itself is not.
  • warnings: a list of warning lines, empty when there are none.
  • smoke_ok: true after a passing --smoke, otherwise null.
  • sbom: the SBOM path with --sbom, otherwise null.
  • scan: with --scan, the finding counts critical, high, medium, low, negligible, unknown and total. Otherwise null.
  • signed: the by-digest reference that --sign signed, otherwise null.
  • packages: see the next section.

docs.title: Name the packages behind the bundled files
docs.text:
Scratchsmith copies libraries from the build host into the image. The image has no package database, so an SBOM of it names almost none of those libraries, and a vulnerability scan cannot see them. The host knows which package owns each of those paths. --packages records that.

--packages takes a comma-separated list of the places the data goes:

Value Where the data goes report A packages list in the --format json report sbom The SBOM (--sbom) names the packages, and the scan (--scan) sees them image The package records stay in the image, for any scanner that reads the image none Nowhere. Scratchsmith looks nothing up. none must be the only value

The default is report,sbom. The default changes no image. Before 2.0 the default was report. To keep that result, set --packages report.

sbom needs a reader. If neither --sbom nor --scan is on, nothing reads the records. Scratchsmith then turns that output off and skips its lookup. If you set sbom yourself, the pack prints a warning. The default sbom goes quietly. The pack does not fail.

The text report does not show the list. So a pack with the text report, and with no --packages value and no packages key, drops the report output. It then runs the lookup only for --sbom or --scan. To fill the list with the text report, name the outputs on the command line or in the configuration file.

scratchsmith pack --format json ./app | jq .packages       # default: the report
scratchsmith pack --sbom --scan ./app                      # default: the SBOM and scan see them
scratchsmith pack --packages report,sbom,image --push ghcr.io/you/app:1.0 ./app
scratchsmith pack --packages none ./app                    # look nothing up

The sbom output can make a scan gate fail. With sbom, the scan sees packages such as glibc and openssl that it did not see before. A pipeline that runs --scan --scan-fail-on high can pass with --packages report and fail with the default. The vulnerabilities were in the image before. The scan did not see them.

docs.title: The report
docs.text:
Each entry names one package and the files in the image that it owns:

{
  "name": "libc6",
  "version": "2.41-12+deb13u4",
  "arch": "amd64",
  "source": "glibc",
  "type": "deb",
  "files": [
    "/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2",
    "/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2",
    "/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6"
  ]
}
  • source is the source package, which is the name that security advisories use.
  • type is deb on a dpkg host and rpm on an rpm host.
  • On an rpm host, version is the version and the release with a hyphen between them, such as 2.34-83.el9.7. If the package has an epoch, the epoch and a colon come first.
  • files are paths in the image. The loader is listed at two paths in this example. The interpreter path holds the one copy, and the other path is a relative symlink to it.
  • The lookup covers the binary, the libraries that it needs, the loader, and the NSS modules. It also covers the files from --tz, --init, --add-file and --add-binary.
  • If --symlinks staged an --add-file entry as a link, that entry is not in the list. A link carries none of the package's content.
  • The --ca-certs bundle is a special case. The host generates that file, so no package owns its path. Scratchsmith names the ca-certificates package for it, because the bundle is built from that package. This one entry is a convention and not a lookup.
  • A locale from --locale is not in the list.
  • A file that no package owns, such as a binary that you built, is not in the list.
  • On a dpkg host, a file whose host path contains *, ?, [ or \ is not in the list. dpkg-query reads those characters as a pattern, so scratchsmith does not ask about that path, and it prints a warning that names the file.
  • Scratchsmith asks which package owns the path. It does not compare the file's contents with the package's. If a file on the host was replaced by hand, the report still names the package.

The packages field is always in the JSON report. Its value tells you what scratchsmith knows:

Value Meaning A list with entries The host named these owners An empty list The host was asked, and no package owns a bundled file null Not reported: the report output is off, the host has no dpkg or rpm database, or the lookup failed

docs.title: The SBOM and the image
docs.text:
For the sbom and image outputs, scratchsmith writes records that scanners already read, and copies the host's /etc/os-release. Syft, grype and other scanners read both. The scanner needs os-release to know the distribution. Without it, a scanner cannot match a package to an advisory.

The records depend on the package manager of the build host:

Host Records dpkg (Debian, Ubuntu and their relatives) One text file for each package, under /var/lib/dpkg/status.d/ rpm (Fedora, RHEL and their relatives) One rpm database that holds only the owning packages, at the host's database path
  • With sbom, those files are in the staged tree only while the SBOM and the scan run. The image does not contain them.
  • With image, they stay, and they count toward --max-size. Your image then has an /etc/os-release that names the build host's distribution. If you add your own /etc/os-release with --add-file, scratchsmith keeps yours. An SBOM of that image names the packages too, because the records are in the tree that syft reads.
  • On an rpm host, the database is about half a megabyte for a small program. The dpkg records are a few kilobytes.
  • On an rpm host that keeps its database in the Berkeley DB format, an image with the records is not reproducible. Rocky Linux 8 and the rest of the RHEL 8 family are such hosts. rpm writes different bytes each time it builds that database, so two packs of the same program give two digests. The pack prints a warning. The report and sbom outputs are not affected.
  • The records need an rpm that has rpmdb --exportdb. rpm 4.11, on CentOS 7 and Amazon Linux 2, does not have it. On those hosts report works and the image output fails. If --sbom or --scan is on, a sbom that you set fails too. The default sbom turns off quietly there. The report still names the packages, and the SBOM and the scan see none.
  • If the pack stages a file, a link or a directory at a path that a record needs, scratchsmith keeps it and does not replace or remove it. It can be a file that you add with --add-file. When the host keeps the program or a library at that path, it can be that file too. A sbom or image that you set then fails the pack, and the error says which output to remove. The default sbom leaves the records out and prints a warning, and the pack goes on. The SBOM and the scan then see no package records.

docs.title: Hosts with no package database
docs.text:
--packages works on a host with a dpkg or an rpm database. What happens on another host depends on what you asked for:

You set Result on a host with neither database Nothing (the default) packages is null, and the SBOM and the scan see no packages. No warning --packages report packages is null, with a warning --packages with image The pack fails. Scratchsmith does not ship an image without the data that you asked for --packages with sbom, and --sbom or --scan The pack fails. Scratchsmith does not ship an SBOM without the data that you asked for --packages with sbom, and neither --sbom nor --scan The pack works and warns. Nothing reads the records, so scratchsmith does not ask for them

If scratchsmith needs the records for one of those outputs and cannot write them, the pack also fails.

scratchsmith doctor tells you before you pack. On an rpm host that cannot write the records, the rpm row starts with warn and names the outputs that fail.

docs.title: Trim the NSS modules
docs.text:
glibc loads name-service (NSS) modules at runtime to resolve names: hostnames to IP addresses, and user or group IDs to names. Scratchsmith stages a default set (local files plus DNS). If your program does fewer lookups, drop the modules it does not need with --nss. Fewer modules mean a smaller image and less code that can carry a CVE.

scratchsmith pack ./app                 # default: local files + DNS
scratchsmith pack --nss files ./app     # local-file lookups only, no DNS
scratchsmith pack --nss none ./app      # no NSS modules, for a program that resolves no names

dns covers hostname resolution only, not the network itself. A program that connects to a raw IP address needs no NSS module. A program that reaches a host by name over TLS also needs CA certificates, which you add separately with --ca-certs. --nss none also skips the generated /etc/nsswitch.conf, and --nss files writes one that lists local files alone. A mode without files also drops /etc/passwd and /etc/group. Because glibc reads them through the files module, user and group lookups do not work there. musl has no NSS, so --nss is refused for a musl binary (see Pack a musl binary).

docs.title: Add a writable /tmp
docs.text:
A scratch image has no /tmp, and many programs exit at startup without one. --tmp adds an empty /tmp, mode 1777 and owned by uid 0, the same as on a Linux host. If a library staged from an RPATH under /tmp already made it, /tmp keeps that library and only its mode is set. The image's non-root user can then write there with no --tmpfs at run time.

scratchsmith pack --tmp ./app

The layer stays reproducible: the directory gets the same mode, owner and mtime on every pack. A --no-build rootfs has the same mode, owned by the user who ran the pack. Files written to /tmp live in the container's writable layer, so mount a --tmpfs instead when the container runs with --read-only.

docs.title: Add a host file
docs.text:
--ca-certs and --tz each add a fixed file (--ca-certs also links /etc/ssl/cert.pem to it). To add any other host file, use --add-file. A scratch image starts empty. A program that reads a configuration file, a template, or a data file at runtime needs that file copied in.

scratchsmith pack --add-file ./app.conf:/etc/app/app.conf ./app   # copy to a chosen path
scratchsmith pack --add-file /etc/motd ./app                      # keep the host path

Write each entry as SRC:DST, where SRC is the host file and DST is the absolute path inside the image. Scratchsmith creates the parent directories of DST. A bare SRC is its own destination, so it must be an absolute path. The flag repeats, and the add-file key in scratchsmith.toml takes the same list.

An added file does not keep its host permission bits. In an image it lands owned by uid 0, with mode 0644. The mode is 0755 for an executable source. The layer writer canonicalizes modes so that the layer stays reproducible. A source at mode 0600 is therefore world-readable inside the image. Do not add a secret this way. Only a --no-build --output rootfs keeps the source bits.

With the default --symlinks copy-all, the flag takes regular files only. If the source is missing or is a directory, the pack fails and names the path. One DST given in two entries is a usage error with exit code 2, so a second entry cannot quietly replace the first. If DST is already in the image for another reason, the pack fails as well. A file you asked for is never skipped without a word. The added files count toward --max-size.

Another --symlinks mode changes two of those rules, and only for a source that is itself a symlink. A preserved link is staged as a link, so a link to a directory no longer fails. Under skip-unsafe an entry the pack cannot honor stages nothing and warns. The section below has the detail.

docs.title: Add a program with its libraries
docs.text:
--add-file copies a file as it is. An ELF program added that way arrives without the shared libraries it needs, so it fails in the image with error while loading shared libraries. --add-binary takes the same SRC[:DST] form and also resolves the program's libraries, with the same loader rules as the packed binary (glibc's or musl's). $ORIGIN in its RPATH or RUNPATH names the real directory of the added file on the host, and the loader reads it from the program's directory in the image. So the pack fails when a program that uses $ORIGIN is given a DST in another directory, and the message names the DST to use.

scratchsmith pack --add-binary /usr/bin/bash:/bin/bash ./app

A library that the packed binary needs too is staged once. The image's ld.so.cache (or, for musl, its search path file and links), --deny and --require, --strip, the SBOM and --packages all cover the added libraries. The added program itself is copied like an --add-file entry, so the same destination rules apply to it. It is always copied as a file, whatever --symlinks says, so a symlinked SRC brings its target's content. One image has one loader, so the pack fails when the added ELF is built for another architecture or names another program interpreter than the packed binary, and when the added program uses the other libc. A static ELF, or a shared library, names no interpreter, so that check passes. A shared library that loads the other libc still fails the pack. A file that is not an ELF fails too: add it with --add-file.

docs.title: Keep a symlink as a symlink
docs.text:
Scratchsmith copies the content of a symlink you name, so the image gets a regular file and not the link. That loses the path itself. If you pack /usr/bin/python3, which is a link to python3.13, the image holds the real file and nothing at /usr/bin/python3. A container that runs the name rather than the target then fails to start. --symlinks chooses what happens instead.

scratchsmith pack --symlinks preserve /usr/bin/python3
Mode What a named symlink becomes copy-all The target's content. An --add-file source gets it at the named path. The packed binary gets it at its real path, with nothing at the named path. This is the default, and the only behavior before 1.4.0. preserve A link. A target outside the image makes it dangle, and the pack warns. copy-unsafe A link for a target inside the image. The target's content for a target outside it. skip-unsafe A link for a target inside the image. Nothing at all for a target outside it, and the pack warns.

The mode covers the packed binary's own path and each --add-file source. Resolved libraries are not in scope, because the loader decides those and the stager already recreates the soname links it needs.

Preserving a link never pulls its target into the image. You add the target yourself, with --add-file, or you accept a link that dangles. The packed binary is the exception: its real file is always staged, so a preserved link to it always resolves. Added files are staged in the order you list them, so a link can point at an earlier --add-file but not at a later one.

docs.title: Stage a locale
docs.text:
A scratch image carries no locale data, so a glibc program runs in the C locale and setlocale fails for any other. --locale stages one compiled locale at /usr/lib/locale/<name>. With no LOCPATH set, glibc reads exactly that path.

scratchsmith pack --locale en_US.UTF-8 --env LANG=en_US.UTF-8 ./app

Name the locale the way glibc names it, such as en_US.UTF-8 or de_DE.UTF-8@euro. Scratchsmith takes the data from a matching directory under /usr/lib/locale on the host. If there is no such directory, it compiles the locale with localedef, which reads the glibc locale sources at /usr/share/i18n. If neither source is available, the pack fails and names what is missing.

The host locale-archive file is never copied. One archive holds every locale the host has. That is hundreds of megabytes on a full distribution, far more than one program needs. A single locale costs about 3 MB, and most of that is the collation table LC_COLLATE.

Staging the data does not select it. Set LANG, LC_ALL, or a per-category entry such as LC_TIME with --env, because the environment is what glibc reads at startup. If you stage a locale and set none of them, the pack warns and the program runs in the C locale. If a selector names a locale the pack did not stage, the pack warns as well. glibc falls back to the C locale for that category. The flag repeats, and the locale key in scratchsmith.toml takes the same list. Locale data counts toward --max-size. musl does not read these locales, so --locale is refused for a musl binary.

docs.title: Pack a musl binary
docs.text:
A dynamic musl program, such as one built on Alpine or with musl-gcc, packs the same way as a glibc one. Scratchsmith sees musl in the binary's loader (/lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1) and resolves the libraries by musl's rules, which Architecture lists. Only x86_64 is supported for now.

scratchsmith pack ./app                      # on Alpine, or with musl's libraries in the host root
scratchsmith pack --format json ./app | jq -e '.libc == "musl"'

What changes for a musl binary:

  • No loader cache. musl reads no ld.so.cache, so pack writes none and does not need ldconfig. An Alpine host has no glibc ldconfig, and that is fine. When a library comes from a directory outside musl's defaults (/lib, /usr/local/lib, /usr/lib), the image gets an /etc/ld-musl-x86_64.path that lists it.
  • No NSS. musl reads /etc/passwd and /etc/group itself, so the image always gets the minimal pair and no NSS module. --nss, or an nss key in scratchsmith.toml, exits 2.
  • No glibc locales. musl has a built-in C.UTF-8 and does not read compiled glibc locales, so --locale, or a locale key, exits 2.
  • One libc per image. An --add-binary program of the other libc fails the pack.
  • --ca-certs. Alpine's OpenSSL and curl read the CA bundle at /etc/ssl/cert.pem, not at /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt. --ca-certs stages the bundle at the second path and links the first to it, as Alpine does, so TLS works with no --cacert flag. A file that --add-file puts at /etc/ssl/cert.pem is kept, and no link is made.
  • --packages. An Alpine host keeps an apk database, which --packages does not read yet. The report says null there, as on any host with no dpkg or rpm database.

docs.title: Inspect the dependency graph
docs.text:
To see the libraries pack resolves for the binary, without building an image, run graph:

scratchsmith graph ./app                            # ASCII tree of the resolved deps
scratchsmith graph --format json ./app              # machine-readable adjacency list
scratchsmith graph --include libplugin.so.1 ./app   # add a dlopen'd library, like pack

The tree shows each library in full the first time. A later repeat is marked (*), so a shared dependency or a cycle does not print twice. A dependency that does not resolve is shown as (missing), and graph then exits with code 1 after it prints the tree. If the binary has a loader (PT_INTERP), the last line names it.

graph shows the binary's own dependency tree and --include. It does not show the NSS modules (libnss_files.so.2, libnss_dns.so.2 and libresolv.so.2 by default) or an --add-binary program and its libraries, which pack also stages. The pack report lists the NSS modules under its payload sizes (size.entries in --format json).

graph --format json prints one object: root (the binary's real path), interpreter (the loader, or null), libc ("glibc", "musl", or null with no loader), nodes and missing (every soname that did not resolve). Each node has id (its real path), name (the soname the loader searched for, the loader's own file name for its node, or the binary's file name), needs (the ids of the nodes it needs) and missing (its own sonames that did not resolve).

docs.title: See each decision with --verbose
docs.text:
To see why a library was picked, or where a file was staged, add --verbose. It works before or after the subcommand:

scratchsmith --verbose pack --no-build -o rootfs ./app
scratchsmith graph --verbose ./app

pack and graph then print one line on standard error for each decision, each starting verbose:. The lines say which directories each object searches, the file each DT_NEEDED name resolves to (or that it is not found, or already loaded), and, for pack, the binary, interpreter, libraries and name-service files it stages, each link it makes, and the directories in the image's /etc/ld.so.cache (for musl, the search path file it writes). Standard output and every other line stay as they are without the flag, so --format json still prints only JSON. The wording of the verbose: lines is for reading, not parsing, and can change in any release.

docs.title: Gate on libraries
docs.text:
To enforce a library policy in CI, fail the pack on a forbidden library or a missing required one:

scratchsmith pack --deny libssl.so.3 ./app        # fail if OpenSSL is staged
scratchsmith pack --require libseccomp.so.2 ./app  # fail if seccomp is missing

Both flags repeat and match exactly, by soname or staged file name. The resolved libraries, the loader, and the NSS modules are all in scope. Read the library names from scratchsmith graph. The NSS modules are not in graph, so read those from the pack report. The same keys work in scratchsmith.toml as deny and require.

docs.title: Diff two builds
docs.text:
To catch image drift, stage two builds and compare their rootfs directories:

scratchsmith pack --no-build --output old ./app-v1
scratchsmith pack --no-build --output new ./app-v2
scratchsmith diff old new              # files added, removed, changed, mode changes, size delta
scratchsmith diff --exit-code old new  # exit non-zero on any difference (a CI gate)

diff marks an added file with +, a removed file with -, and a changed file with ~. It also compares permission bits: a regular file or directory in both trees whose mode differs prints as ~ path (mode 0755 -> 0644), so a lost exec bit or a world-writable directory fails --exit-code. A symlink has no mode of its own, so only its target is compared. An empty directory in only one tree prints as + path/ (empty directory) or - path/ (empty directory). A directory that holds anything shows through the files in it. diff then prints the total size delta. --format json emits the same data for a machine: added and removed (each entry has path and size), changed (a list of paths), mode_changed (each with path, before and after as four octal digits), the empty directories in dirs_added and dirs_removed, and the total file bytes of each tree in size_before and size_after.

A staged rootfs keeps the modes from the host: a directory gets its mode from the umask, and a file keeps the mode of its source. The image layer rewrites them, to 0755 for a directory and 0755 or 0644 for a file by its exec bit. So two staged trees from builders with different umasks, or with a binary at 0775 on one and 0755 on the other, differ in mode although their images are the same. A sticky directory such as the --tmp /tmp keeps 1777 in the layer. Stage both builds on one builder, or compare the modes that ship: unpack both images and diff those trees, which carry the layer's modes.

A file name that is not valid UTF-8 is escaped whole, in both the text and the JSON output: its invalid bytes become \xNN, and a backslash, a quote or a control character in it is escaped too.

Both arguments must be directories. A file argument, such as an OCI archive, is read as an empty tree and prints a deprecation warning. 3.0 refuses it. To compare two archives, unpack each one first.

docs.title: Unpack an image
docs.text:
To audit an image you did not build, extract its OCI archive to a directory:

scratchsmith unpack app.oci.tar ./rootfs   # apply the layers into ./rootfs

unpack reads an OCI-layout archive (what pack --oci-archive writes, or a skopeo/buildah export), applies each layer in order, and honors whiteouts. Combine it with diff to compare two images: unpack both, then run scratchsmith diff old new. When a later layer holds an entry for a path that exists, unpack replaces that path, as a container runtime does. A directory over a directory keeps its contents. A symlink inside the image resolves against the target directory as the image's /, so a file under Debian's var/run -> /run lands in run/. unpack refuses, and exits 1, an entry or hard link that would leave the target. When the archive's index lists more than one manifest, unpack applies only the first, and prints a warning on standard error that names its digest, and its platform when the index gives one.

unpack reads every gzip member of a layer, as Docker does. It refuses a layer that is cut short, has data after its end, or holds a sparse entry, an entry with a .. part, a hard link above the image root or a malformed PAX record, and exits 1 before that layer writes or deletes any file. A layer may hold at most 2 GiB once decompressed, and all layers together at most 16 GiB. A layer that the manifest lists twice counts twice.

unpack writes each entry relative to the directory that holds it, so an entry deeper than the host's path limit (4096 bytes) unpacks. It reaches that directory through /proc, which a container runtime mounts by default. Without /proc, unpack fails and names the entry.

unpack clears the setuid and setgid bits on every file and directory it writes. An untrusted image cannot then plant a setuid program owned by the user who unpacks it. unpack prints one warning line on standard error for each path in the final image that had one of those bits. The stripped_setid field of --format json lists the same paths. The other fields are source (the archive), dir (where it was extracted), layers (how many were applied) and files (how many files and symlinks were written).

unpack applies the mode of each directory after the last layer, so a directory without owner write permission, such as /root in a Fedora image, unpacks for a user who is not root. Until then such a directory stays open to its owner, so a failed unpack leaves a tree that its owner can remove. A finished tree keeps the image's modes, so it may need chmod -R u+w before rm -rf.

docs.title: Multi-arch images
docs.text:
Scratchsmith resolves against the host's libraries, so it packs for the architecture it runs on. To publish a multi-arch image, run pack --push on each architecture (a CI matrix). Then combine the per-arch images into one multi-arch OCI image index with index. That is the daemonless equivalent of docker manifest create, with no Docker or buildx:

# on the amd64 runner
scratchsmith pack --push ghcr.io/you/app:1.0-amd64 ./app
# on the arm64 runner
scratchsmith pack --push ghcr.io/you/app:1.0-arm64 ./app

# then, once both are pushed, assemble the index that consumers pull by one tag
scratchsmith index ghcr.io/you/app:1.0 \
  ghcr.io/you/app:1.0-amd64 \
  ghcr.io/you/app:1.0-arm64

Each source's platform is read from its own image configuration. Nothing is rebuilt, and no cross-arch resolution happens. The sources must already be pushed, and must live in the target's repository. An index references its children by digest within one repository, so this is typically the same repo with a different tag, as above. Add --sign to cosign-sign the index by digest.

index --format json prints one object with four fields:

  • pushed: the target reference, as you gave it.
  • manifests: one entry per source, in the order you gave them. Each entry has source (the reference as you gave it), platform (such as linux/amd64, read from the source's image configuration) and digest (the child manifest's sha256: digest).
  • signed: the by-digest reference that --sign signed, or null without --sign.
  • warnings: a list of warnings about the push, such as a registry that answered with another digest. It is empty when there are none. With --sign, a digest mismatch fails the command instead, so warnings stays empty.

docs.title: Image metadata and entrypoint
docs.text:
Set what the image runs: entrypoint, arguments, environment, working directory, and user:

scratchsmith pack /opt/app/bin/app \
  --cmd serve --env LANG=C.UTF-8 --workdir /data --user 65532:65532 \
  --label role=api --healthcheck /opt/app/bin/app --healthcheck --health

The packed binary keeps its host path in the image (its real path, after symlinks), and that path is the default entrypoint. So an --entrypoint or --healthcheck that runs the binary must name that path. Scratchsmith does not check either one.

--healthcheck (like --cmd) is repeatable, and each token is one argument of a single exec command. So --healthcheck /opt/app/bin/app --healthcheck --health is the one command ["/opt/app/bin/app", "--health"], not two healthchecks. It is the same as healthcheck = ["/opt/app/bin/app", "--health"] in the configuration file.

Each --env and --label entry needs an =. An entry with no = is an error with exit code 2. To set an empty value, end the entry with =, as in --label build=.

docs.title: Pack again on every change
docs.text:
While you develop the program that you pack, --watch packs it again after each build. It packs one time, and then packs again each time the binary changes:

scratchsmith pack --watch ./target/release/app

Scratchsmith looks at the binary two times each second. After a change, it waits until the file is the same on two looks in a row. That keeps most half-written binaries out. If the linker stalls for longer, the pack of the half-written file fails, and the finished file packs next. If the binary is gone for five seconds, scratchsmith says so one time and continues to watch.

Each pack prints its text report. To stop, press Ctrl-C. Scratchsmith does not catch the interrupt, so the exit status is the one your shell gives a process that Ctrl-C ended.

Only the binary is watched. A change to a library or to an --add-file source does not start a pack. The next pack that the binary starts picks it up. A change to the configuration file is not picked up at all, because scratchsmith reads that file one time. Stop the watch and start it again.

If the first pack fails, the command exits with an error, the same as a pack with no --watch. If a later pack fails, scratchsmith prints the error and continues to watch. A build that fails halfway does not end the watch.

--watch works with the default load and with --oci-archive. It refuses three things:

  • --push, and a push key from the configuration file unless --oci-archive replaces it. A registry is not the place for an image from every save.
  • --no-build. That sink stages into one directory, and a second pack into the same directory is an error, because the directory is no longer empty.
  • --format json. Each pack prints a text report.

--watch is a command-line flag only. It has no key in the configuration file and no input on the GitHub Action.

docs.title: In CI
docs.text: To pack in a GitHub Actions workflow with the composite action instead of shelling out to the CLI, see GitHub Action.

docs.title: Run pack in a container — the :toolbox image
docs.text:
The FROM scratch release image carries the binary and nothing else: no shell, no tools, and no certificate store. It runs every subcommand that needs no external tool. That is lint, doctor, graph, diff, unpack, and index without --sign, plus the --version and --completions flags. doctor is the one that looks like an exception: it probes for each external tool and reports every one as missing, which is the right answer on an image that carries none.

index reaches a registry over HTTPS, which needs a list of trusted certificate authorities. On a host with a certificate store, scratchsmith uses that store. This image has none, so scratchsmith uses the Mozilla root certificates that are compiled into the binary. It prints one warning to standard error to say so. To use your own certificates, mount a PEM file and set SSL_CERT_FILE to its path. A registry behind a proxy that inspects TLS needs that.

The compiled-in certificates are as new as the scratchsmith release that carries them. A certificate store on the host gets updates from the operating system. The compiled-in set changes only with a newer scratchsmith release.

Scratchsmith reads the compiled-in certificates through /proc. A container runtime mounts /proc by default. Without it, the command fails and says so.

If SSL_CERT_FILE or SSL_CERT_DIR is set, scratchsmith never uses the compiled-in certificates. If the path that you set gives no certificates, the command fails and names the variable.

Two subcommands do not run there. pack needs ldconfig for a glibc binary, plus a container engine for the default sink and strip, syft or grype for the options that use them. verify needs cosign. The :toolbox image below runs both.

The :toolbox image bundles the pack toolchain (ldconfig, strip, syft, grype, cosign, upx, tini, the docker CLI) on a Wolfi base. With it, pack itself runs inside a container. Wolfi is glibc-based and has no musl loader, so the toolbox packs glibc binaries only. That image has no dpkg and no rpm database, so --packages has no data there. The packages field is null. An image output that you set fails. If --sbom or --scan is on, a sbom output that you set fails too. The default stays quiet.

# Daemonless — no socket needed; write an OCI archive or push straight to a registry.
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/w" -w /w ghcr.io/schubydoo/scratchsmith:toolbox \
  pack --oci-archive app.oci.tar ./app
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/w" -w /w \
  -v "$HOME/.docker:/docker:ro" -e DOCKER_CONFIG=/docker \
  ghcr.io/schubydoo/scratchsmith:toolbox pack --push ghcr.io/you/app:1.0 ./app

--push reads the registry login from the Docker config, so mount one that holds the credentials themselves. A credential helper on the host is not available inside the container.

Prefer the daemonless sinks (--push / --oci-archive) in CI. The default docker load sink needs a host engine, so mount its socket. That socket is root-equivalent on the host, so use it only where you trust the workflow:

docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock -v "$PWD:/w" -w /w \
  ghcr.io/schubydoo/scratchsmith:toolbox pack ./app

Tags: :toolbox (latest), :X.Y.Z-toolbox, :X.Y-toolbox. Verify its signature exactly like the scratch image. See Verifying releases.

docs.title: Verifying releases
docs.text:
Release artifacts are keyless-signed (cosign) and carry a SLSA build-provenance attestation, at Build Level 3 from v2.2.0 on. Each release from v1.0.0 on also ships a CycloneDX SBOM of Scratchsmith's own dependency graph. That file is scratchsmith-v<ver>.cdx.json, and it is listed in checksums.txt, so the signature and provenance cover it too. It reflects the full Cargo.lock graph, so it includes build- and dev-dependencies, not only the crates that link into the shipped binary.

The release also carries scratchsmith.intoto.jsonl, the SLSA provenance bundle. You do not need to download it, because gh attestation verify reads the attestation from GitHub. That needs gh signed in (gh auth login). To check against the bundle instead, see Verifying from the bundle.

Replace <ver> with the bare version you downloaded, no leading v (the tarball adds the v prefix, but the image tag does not).

The provenance is Build Level 3 because the binaries are built and attested inside a reusable workflow, release-binaries.yml, which signs the provenance with its own identity. The release workflow that calls it can't add steps to its jobs. --signer-workflow checks for that identity, so a provenance signed by any other workflow in the repository fails the check. v2.2.0 is the first release built this way. v2.1.0 and older carry Build Level 2 provenance, signed by knope-release.yml. For those, leave out --signer-workflow.

The Build Level 3 provenance covers the tarballs and the SBOM, not the GHCR image. The image packs the same release binaries. It carries its own cosign signature, which the cosign verify command below checks, and BuildKit provenance and SBOM attestations in the registry, which are not Level 3.

# SLSA Build L3 provenance — the simplest, ref-agnostic check
gh attestation verify scratchsmith-v<ver>-linux-amd64.tar.gz --repo schubydoo/scratchsmith \
  --signer-workflow schubydoo/scratchsmith/.github/workflows/release-binaries.yml

# Checksums signature (one cosign signature covers every tarball through its hash)
cosign verify-blob checksums.txt \
  --bundle checksums.txt.sigstore.json \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/schubydoo/scratchsmith/\.github/workflows/knope-release\.yml@' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
sha256sum -c --ignore-missing checksums.txt   # then check the hashes of the files you downloaded

# The signed GHCR image
cosign verify ghcr.io/schubydoo/scratchsmith:<ver> \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/schubydoo/scratchsmith/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@refs/tags/' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

docs.title: Verifying from the bundle
docs.text:
To check the provenance against the scratchsmith.intoto.jsonl that ships in the release, instead of fetching it from GitHub, pass it with --bundle:

gh attestation verify scratchsmith-v<ver>-linux-amd64.tar.gz --repo schubydoo/scratchsmith \
  --bundle scratchsmith.intoto.jsonl \
  --signer-workflow schubydoo/scratchsmith/.github/workflows/release-binaries.yml

gh still fetches Sigstore's trusted root. For a machine with no network, save it first on one that has it, with gh attestation trusted-root > trusted_root.jsonl, and add --custom-trusted-root trusted_root.jsonl.

docs.title: Rebuilding a release binary
docs.text: Release binaries from v2.2.0 on are reproducible. For every such release, a CI job rebuilds both binaries from the tag and checks that they match the published ones byte for byte. To run the same check yourself, follow REPRODUCE.md.

docs.title: Verifying an image you signed with pack
docs.text:
The commands above verify Scratchsmith's own release artifacts. To sign an image Scratchsmith builds for you, pack --push --sign cosign-signs the pushed image by digest (keyless), and --sbom --sign attaches the SBOM as a signed attestation. Both only apply to the registry-push sink, since cosign signs a registry image. See Usage.

Scratchsmith runs cosign sign and cosign attest with no key, so the signature carries the OIDC identity of whoever ran --sign. Verify with the identity and issuer of that signer:

Where --sign ran --certificate-identity --certificate-oidc-issuer GitHub Actions (id-token: write) https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/.github/workflows/<file>@<ref> https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com Your terminal, signed in with Google your email address https://accounts.google.com

For a terminal login with another provider, the identity is still your email, and the issuer is that provider's. Sigstore's verification cheat sheet lists them. In CI, --certificate-identity-regexp lets one check hold for every branch or tag of the workflow.

docs.title: With scratchsmith verify
docs.text:
scratchsmith verify runs both checks below with cosign (cosign must be installed). It takes cosign's names for the identity and issuer flags:

scratchsmith verify ghcr.io/you/app@sha256:... \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/you/app/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  --sbom
  • Identity: give exactly one of --certificate-identity (an exact value) and --certificate-identity-regexp. A pattern must start with ^. cosign matches a pattern anywhere in the identity, so without the anchor a longer identity that contains it passes too.
  • --sbom: also checks the SBOM attestation, of the type that --sbom-format names (cyclonedx-json by default, the same values as pack). Leave it out for an image signed with no SBOM, or for an index.
  • A tag: verify reads the digest the tag points to once, and cosign checks that digest. The report prints it and notes that a tag can move.
  • An index that index --sign signed: verify checks the signature on the index. It does not check the images that the index lists, and --sbom is refused.

It exits 0 when every check passed, 1 when a check failed or could not run (for example the image is not found), and 2 when the command line is refused. --format json prints requested (the reference as given), image (the digest reference that cosign checked), kind (image or index), identity, identity_is_regexp, issuer, signature and attestation (the type checked, or null). A failure prints no report.

A pass proves who signed that image digest. It does not prove that the image is safe, or that the SBOM is complete.

docs.title: With cosign directly
docs.text:
IMAGE=ghcr.io/you/app:latest   # or the @sha256:... reference that the pack printed

# The signature that --sign made
cosign verify "$IMAGE" \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/you/app/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

# The SBOM attestation that --sbom --sign made (CycloneDX, the default --sbom-format)
cosign verify-attestation "$IMAGE" --type cyclonedx \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/you/app/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com > /dev/null

With --sbom-format spdx-json, use --type spdxjson. Pass a tag only if you trust it not to move. The digest reference that the pack printed (signed ...@sha256:..., or the signed field in --format json) pins the exact image. To read the attested SBOM, drop the > /dev/null and decode its payload:

cosign verify-attestation "$IMAGE" --type cyclonedx <identity flags as above> \
  | jq -r .payload | base64 -d | jq .predicate

Scratchsmith's push-auth-smoke workflow runs the same cosign verify and cosign verify-attestation checks, and scratchsmith verify, with its own workflow identity, against an image it packs, pushes to GHCR and signs.
